tail.summary: An open agentic dev environment whose distinguishing features are session goals (the agent keeps working toward a defined finish line turn after turn, even with the app closed), multi-run fusion across up to five models with the option to keep the best or fuse the strongest parts, and prompts on a cron schedule. It also does issue-to-PR flows and moves between desktop, browser, phone and VS Code without losing session state. Serves over a local port with an optional UI password gate and tunnel.

tail.title: TheoremDB: a shared record so research agents stop repeating each other's failed proofs
tail.summary: An alpha public workspace for machine mathematics where each open problem opens a packet showing what has been proved, which routes failed, and the code behind every computation. Solutions are submitted at graded evidence levels, with a Lean-verified proof receiving the highest grade; public writes and Lean contributions are live while semantic expansion is disabled. The stated ambition is to be for mathematical research what OEIS is for integer sequences.

tail.title: How I use LLMs to learn: make the model build a playable simulation of the topic
tail.summary: Rather than asking for an explanation (which the author finds too simplistic and emoji-laden), the flow is: in plan mode ask the model to build a foundational knowledge base for the topic, ask it to audit that base for accuracy, then have it build a low-poly Rollercoaster-Tycoon-style interactive simulation of the process, with responsive layout and pause controls, and publish it to GitHub Pages. Worked example: semiconductor fab process, learned while investigating AI data-centre bottlenecks.

tail.title: JFK's AI voice
tail.summary: Alex Tabarrok posts AI-generated Kennedy readings of the 1961 inaugural, the 1962 Rice moon speech, and Johnson's inaugural passage about Kennedy's death, as a demonstration of where synthetic historical voice has landed. Short post, no argument attached, offered as an artefact.

tail.title: An OpenAI strategist argues AI labs should rival government power
tail.summary: Coverage of an OpenAI strategist making the explicit case that frontier labs should hold power comparable to states rather than accepting a regulated-industry posture. Aggregator write-up, so treat the framing as secondary reporting rather than a primary statement, but it sits directly alongside this week's slowdown-verification and pacing-the-frontier arguments.

tail.title: Incentives are for losers
tail.summary: Adam Mastroianni's argument against the standard social-science move of explaining behaviour by pointing at incentives, on the grounds that incentive explanations are unfalsifiable after the fact and describe what a system rewards rather than what people actually do. Directly relevant to reading any paper whose mechanism section is 'the incentives were misaligned'.

tail.title: CSS: the bomb inside your inbox
tail.summary: PortSwigger research on attacks delivered purely through CSS in HTML email, exploiting the gap between what mail clients sanitise (scripts, most attributes) and what they permit in stylesheets. Relevant to anyone building agents that ingest email, since the sanitisation assumptions that protect a human reader do not necessarily protect a parser.

tail.title: Everything you do is being recorded
tail.summary: On always-on AI wearables and the social norms that have not formed around them, resurfacing on HN this weekend. The relevant thread for human-AI interaction work is consent asymmetry: the wearer opts in, everyone in the room does not, and the recording is the input to a model rather than an archive anyone reviews.

tail.title: Taxi drivers rarely die of Alzheimer's, and complex navigation may be why
tail.summary: A write-up of occupational-mortality data showing taxi and ambulance drivers, whose work demands continuous real-time spatial computation, have unusually low Alzheimer's death rates, unlike bus drivers and pilots who follow fixed routes. The proposed mechanism is hippocampal load from route construction rather than route following. Included as a cognitive-reserve datapoint, with the usual confounding caveats about occupational selection.

tail.title: Silicon Valley misreads its own science fiction, says Jill Lepore
tail.summary: Historian Jill Lepore's argument that the tech industry reads science fiction as a roadmap rather than as the warning most of it was written to be, and that the misreading has downstream consequences for democratic accountability. A useful corrective to the genre of AI-risk argument that borrows its imagery from fiction without noticing the fiction was an indictment.

tail.title: Devs to Anthropic, OpenAI and Cursor: make security and privacy the default
tail.summary: Register coverage of developer pushback demanding that coding-agent vendors ship secure-and-private defaults rather than opt-in hardening, landing the same week Anthropic announced auto mode becomes the default. The two stories read against each other: the default is moving toward less friction while the ask is for it to move the other way.

tail.title: The AI apocalypse is already here
tail.summary: An essay arguing the interesting harms are not the future extinction scenarios but the present-tense degradations of institutions, labour and epistemics that are already measurable. Included as the counterweight to this week's existential-risk and warning-shot cluster, since it disputes not the risk estimate but which timeframe deserves attention.

tail.title: Amazon circumvented a community vote to site an AI data centre in Gilroy
tail.summary: Reporting that Amazon routed around a local Gilroy, California community vote to secure an AI data-centre site. Adds a procedural-capture case to the ongoing data-centre siting fights, which are currently the most concrete place AI infrastructure meets democratic process.

tail.title: Show HN: a source-level review of Sakana AI's Continuous Thought Machine
tail.summary: A line-by-line reading of the Continuous Thought Machine implementation against the claims in Sakana's paper, checking whether the described mechanism is what the code actually does. The genre matters more than the verdict: reproducibility auditing of a released architecture at source level is rare and is the same move as auditing an eval harness rather than trusting its reported scores.

tail.title: Deakin's AI institute is exempt from the scholarship deadline entirely and takes applications year-round
tail.summary: BIGGEST STRUCTURAL FIND OF THE RUN, and it sits inside the university whose round date has resisted verification for five sessions. Deakin's own RTP/DUPRS page carries the sentence 'These deadlines do not apply to applicants for the Institute for Frontier Materials, the Institute for Intelligent Systems Research and Innovation, or the Applied Artificial Intelligence Initiative, who can apply at any time' — meaning the 23 August international close is IRRELEVANT to an A2I2 application. Closing date for internationals: none, rolling all year. Funding: the scholarship attached is the same RTP/DUPRS package (index-derived $37,450 p.a. stipend, 2026 rate, tax exempt, plus tuition), so fees are covered and OSHC is available per Deakin policy doc 222, but this has not been page-read. Entry requires a minimum four-year undergraduate degree in computer science or a related discipline — no research masters. Supervisor: effectively required, but the route is designed for it — you email a2i2_hdr@deakin.edu.au or the project supervisor directly, then interview. INDEX-DERIVED, not a page read: deakin.edu.au and a2i2.deakin.edu.au both serve a bot challenge.

tail.title: Sydney's international RTP re-verified with a full four-round calendar, two of them still ahead
tail.summary: Re-verified on Sydney's own page and the published table now runs four rounds deep, which is unusual generosity on this board. International closes 11 September 2026 for Research Periods 1-2 2027 (32 days), then 18 December 2026 for RP 3-4 2027, then 10 September 2027 for RP 1-2 2028, then mid-December 2027. Outcomes for the September round issue 10 November and finalise 17 December. Funding: $42,754 per annum stipend (2026 rate) under either the RTP Stipend or USYDIS, plus 100% tuition fees for up to 14 research periods awarded automatically alongside the stipend, plus OSHC under the RTP Fee Offset, plus relocation and thesis allowances — second-richest package after RMIT and one of only three doors where fees AND OSHC are both explicitly confirmed. Eligibility does not name a research masters as a prerequisite. Supervisor: the scholarship page is silent but Sydney HDR admission requires an academic supervisor to accept the project, so it gates on supervision in practice. Two-part submission: admission through Sydney Courses AND a separate scholarship form, both by 11 September.

tail.title: Swinburne's Round 2 needs a supervisor's signature on the proposal, a harder gate than last read suggested

Funding: $35,500 per annum stipend (2026 rate, indexed) for three years with a possible six-month extension, plus automatic tuition cover for up to four years — internationals receive a Tuition Fee Scholarship, domestics an RTP Fees-Offset. OSHC is not mentioned. Honours is sufficient: 'a Bachelor Degree with First Class Honours (or equivalent)'. Income restriction: no other living-cost income above 75% of the stipend. The round does not open for four weeks, so there is clear air to secure the signature first.

Second, the International Postgraduate Tuition Awards that would otherwise cover fees run windows of 4 January to 14 February and 1 June to 14 July, both now shut, cover tuition only with no stipend and no OSHC, and require applicants to be CURRENT UOW students, with the supervisor accessing the form on the candidate's behalf. tail.title: Western Sydney's research round requires an MPhil earned at Western Sydney itself, which disqualifies outside applicants

Honours alone is not sufficient here, and applications 'must include a letter of support from a suitable supervisor'. Western Sydney should be treated as closed to this profile structurally, not just for this cycle.

Aggregator reporting puts it at three or more fully funded places at roughly $37,000 per annum; that figure is not confirmed on Murdoch's own page and neither fees nor OSHC are stated. Recorded for two reasons that outlast the deadline. First, it establishes that an ARC-funded Research Hub explicitly badged 'Responsible AI' exists and is recruiting in Australia, which is a category of funding this board had not previously surfaced and which will run for years. Second, it shows the pattern to watch: hub-attached scholarships appear on a university's scholarship index with about four weeks of notice and no international/domestic split, so they are only catchable by checking indexes weekly. The applied domain here is agriculture, so fit is poor regardless — but the hub structure is worth tracking for AI-evaluation-shaped calls.

tail.title: Canberra pays a stipend to internationals but will only 'may' cover their tuition, and publishes no HDR round dates at all
tail.summary: New to the board and left honestly incomplete. UC offers University Research Scholarships to domestic and international candidates at $36,225 per annum tax-free (2025 rate, the most recent published), applied for through the HDR portal in two stages — admission first, then a separate scholarship form. Honours is sufficient and priority goes to 'An Australian First-Class Honours result, or a qualification or Recognised Prior Learning (RPL) considered equivalent', with RPL an unusually explicit door for non-standard backgrounds. Two problems. First, fee cover is discretionary, not automatic: 'International candidates may also be awarded a tuition fee waiver' — 'may', not 'will' — and OSHC is not mentioned anywhere. Second, NO CLOSING DATE IS PUBLISHED for either international or domestic applicants; the scholarships page defers to a key-dates page which turns out to carry no HDR rows at all, only coursework semester dates. UC also withholds the stipend from internationals until they are physically onshore, then back-pays. Days-left is genuinely unknown; this needs a call to the Student Centre before it can be planned around.

tail.title: CSIRO Data61's student scholarship pages are gone, returning 410 rather than a closure notice
tail.summary: Swept as a named target and the result is a dead end rather than a deadline. Both Data61 student-program pages — the scholarship page and its project list — return HTTP 410 Gone, which is the server explicitly stating the resource has been permanently removed rather than merely moved. The legacy data61.csiro.au scholarship URL 301-redirects to a generic CSIRO technology-and-space landing page, and the csiro.au careers path for Data61 scholarships 404s. What the search index still records of the program: it was a TOP-UP award only, requiring the candidate to already hold a government, university or third-party base stipend from an Australian university, advertised through CSIRO's recruitment portal only while open. Since it can never be the primary funding instrument, its absence costs nothing structurally — but it does mean the standing assumption that a Data61 top-up can be stacked on an RTP stipend can no longer be relied on without asking CSIRO directly. No closing date, no amount, no eligibility statement is currently retrievable.
